stem: A resistance thermometer has resistance 95.2 \(\Omega\) at the ice point and 138.6 \(\Omega\) at the steam point. What resistance would be obtained if the actual temperature is 27 \(^\circ\)C?
solution:
Here the thermometric property P is the resistance. Using Eq. (7.2), if R is the resistance at 27 \(^\circ\)C, we have

\(27 = \dfrac{100(R - 95.2)}{(138.6 - 95.2)}\)

\(\therefore R = \dfrac{27 \times (138.6 - 95.2)}{100} + 95.2\)

\(= 11.72 + 95.2 = 106.92\ \Omega\)

stem: Calculate the temperature which has the same value on fahernheit scale and kelvin scale.
solution:
Let the required temperature be \(y\). i.e., \(T_{F} = T_{K} = y\) then we have

\(\dfrac{y - 32}{180} = \dfrac{y - 273.15}{100}\)

or, \(5y - 160 = 9y - 2458.35\)

or, \(4y = -160 + 2458.35\)

\(\therefore y = 574.59\)

Thus 574.59 \(^\circ\)F and 574.59 K are equivalent temperatures.
_note: The book misspells 'fahrenheit' as 'fahernheit' in the printed stem; transcribed verbatim. Working and answer are correct (4y = 2298.35, y = 574.5875).

stem: The pressure reading in a thermometer at steam point is \(1.367 \times 10^{3}\) Pa. What is pressure reading at triple point knowing the linear relationship between temperature and pressure?
solution:
We have \(P_{\text{triple}} = 273.16 \times \left(\dfrac{P}{T}\right)\) where \(P_{\text{triple}}\) and \(P\) are the pressures at temperature of triple point (273.16 K) and \(T\) respectively. We are given that \(P = 1.367 \times 10^{3}\) Pa at steam point i.e., at \(273.15 + 100 = 373.15\) K.

\(\therefore P_{\text{triple}} = 273.16 \times \left(\dfrac{1.367 \times 10^{3}}{373.15}\right)\)

\(= 1.000 \times 10^{3}\) Pa

stem: The length of a metal rod at 27 \(^\circ\)C is 4 cm. The length increases to 4.02 cm when the metal rod is heated upto 387 \(^\circ\)C. Determine the coefficient of linear expansion of the metal rod.

Length of an iron rod at temperature 27 \(^\circ\)C is 4.256 m. Find the temperature at which the length of the same rod increases to 4.268 m. (\(\alpha\) for iron \(= 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\) K\(^{-1}\))
A thin aluminium plate has an area 286 cm\(^{2}\) at 20 \(^\circ\)C. Find its area when it is heated to 180 \(^\circ\)C. (\(\beta\) for aluminium \(= 4.9 \times 10^{-5}\) /\(^\circ\)C)

A liquid at 0 \(^\circ\)C is poured in a glass beaker of volume 600 cm\(^{3}\) to fill it completely. The beaker is then heated to 90 \(^\circ\)C. How much liquid will overflow? (\(\gamma_{\text{liquid}} = 1.75 \times 10^{-4}\) /\(^\circ\)C, \(\gamma_{\text{glass}} = 2.75 \times 10^{-5}\) /\(^\circ\)C)
solution:
Given

\(V_{1} = 600\) cm\(^{3}\)

\(T_{1} = 0\ ^\circ\)C

\(T_{2} = 90\ ^\circ\)C

We have \(\gamma = \dfrac{V_{2} - V_{1}}{V_{1}(T_{2} - T_{1})}\)

\(\therefore\) increase is volume \(= V_{2} - V_{1} = \gamma V_{1}(T_{2} - T_{1})\)

Increase in volume of beaker

\(= \gamma_{\text{glass}} \times V_{1}(T_{2} - T_{1})\)

\(= 2.75 \times 10^{-5} \times 600 \times (90 - 0)\)

\(= 2.75 \times 10^{-5} \times 600 \times 90\)

\(= 148500 \times 10^{-5}\) cm\(^{3}\)

\(\therefore\) increase in volume of beaker \(= 1.485\) cm\(^{3}\)

Increase in volume of liquid

\(= \gamma_{\text{liquid}} \times V_{1}(T_{2} - T_{1})\)

\(= 1.75 \times 10^{-4} \times 600 \times (90 - 0)\)

\(= 1.75 \times 10^{-4} \times 600 \times 90\)

\(= 94500 \times 10^{-4}\) cm\(^{3}\)

\(\therefore\) increase in volume of liquid \(= 9.45\) cm\(^{3}\)

\(\therefore\) volume of liquid which overflows

\(= (9.45 - 1.485)\) cm\(^{3}\)

\(= 7.965\) cm\(^{3}\)
_note: The book prints 'increase is volume' for 'increase in volume' in its own solution; kept verbatim. Arithmetic is correct.

stem: A sheet of brass is 50 cm long and 8 cm broad at 0 \(^\circ\)C. If the surface area at 100 \(^\circ\)C is 401.57 cm\(^{2}\), find the coefficient of linear expansion of brass.
solution:
Given

\(T_{1} = 0\ ^\circ\)C

\(T_{2} = 100\ ^\circ\)C

\(A_{1} = 50 \times 8 = 400\) cm\(^{2}\)

\(A_{2} = 401.57\) cm\(^{2}\)

We have

\(\beta = 2\alpha = \dfrac{A_{2} - A_{1}}{A_{1}(T_{2} - T_{1})}\)

\(= \dfrac{(401.57 - 400)\ \text{cm}^{2}}{400\ \text{cm}^{2} \times (100 - 0)\ ^\circ\text{C}}\)

\(= \dfrac{1.57}{400 \times 100} = 0.3925 \times 10^{-4}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)

\(\therefore \alpha = 0.1962 \times 10^{-4}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)

\(= 1.962 \times 10^{-5}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)

\(\therefore\) Coefficient of linear expansion of brass is \(1.962 \times 10^{-5}\) /\(^\circ\)C.

stem: If the temperature of 4 kg mass of a material of specific heat capacity 300 J/kg \(^\circ\)C rises from 20 \(^\circ\)C to 30 \(^\circ\)C. Find the heat received.
solution:
\(Q = 4\ \text{kg} \times (30 - 20)\ ^\circ\text{C} \times 300\ \text{J/kg}\ ^\circ\text{C}\)

\(= 4 \times 10 \times 300\) J

\(\therefore Q = 12000\) J

stem: Find thermal capacity for a copper block of mass 0.2 kg, if specific heat capacity of copper is 290 J/kg \(^\circ\)C.
solution:
Given

\(m = 0.2\) kg

\(s = 290\) J/kg \(^\circ\)C

Thermal capacity \(= m \times s = 0.2\ \text{kg} \times 290\ \text{J/kg}\ ^\circ\text{C}\)

\(= 58\) J/\(^\circ\)C

stem: A sphere of aluminium of 0.06 kg is placed for sufficient time in a vessel containing boiling water so that the sphere is at 100 \(^\circ\)C. It is then immediately transferred to 0.12 kg copper calorimeter containing 0.30 kg of water at 25 \(^\circ\)C. The temperature of water rises and attains a steady state at 28 \(^\circ\)C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium. (Specific heat capacity of water, \(s_{w} = 4.18 \times 10^{3}\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\), specific heat capacity of copper \(s_{Cu} = 0.387 \times 10^{3}\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\))
solution:
Given

Mass of aluminium sphere \(= m_{1} = 0.06\) kg

Mass of copper calorimeter \(= m_{2} = 0.12\) kg

Mass of water in calorimeter \(= m_{3} = 0.30\) kg

Specific heat capacity of copper \(= s_{Cu} = s_{2} = 0.387 \times 10^{3}\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\)

Specific heat capacity of water \(= s_{w} = s_{3} = 4.18 \times 10^{3}\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\)

Initial temperature of aluminium sphere \(= T_{1} = 100\ ^\circ\)C

Initial temperature of calorimeter and water \(= T_{2} = 25\ ^\circ\)C

Final temperature of the mixture \(= T = 28\ ^\circ\)C

We have

\(s_{1} = \dfrac{(m_{2}s_{2} + m_{3}s_{3})(T - T_{2})}{m_{1}(T_{1} - T)}\)

\(= \dfrac{\left[(0.12 \times 387) + (0.30 \times 4180)\right](28 - 25)}{(0.06)(100 - 28)}\)

\(= \dfrac{(46.44 + 1254) \times 3}{(0.06) \times 72} = \dfrac{3901.32}{4.32}\)

\(= 903.08\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\)

\(\therefore\) Specific heat capacity of aluminium is 903.08 J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\).
_note: Solution spans the page break p-14 -> p-15; the printed working completes on p-15. Arithmetic verified correct.

stem: When 0.1 kg of ice at 0 \(^\circ\)C is mixed with 0.32 kg of water at 35 \(^\circ\)C in a container. The resulting temperature of the mixture is 7.8 \(^\circ\)C. Calculate the heat of fusion of ice (\(s_{water} = 4186\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\)).
solution:
Given

\(m_{\text{ice}} = 0.1\) kg

\(m_{\text{water}} = 0.32\) kg

\(T_{\text{ice}} = 0\ ^\circ\)C

\(T_{\text{water}} = 35\ ^\circ\)C

\(T_{F} = 7.8\ ^\circ\)C

\(s_{\text{water}} = 4186\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\)

Heat lost by water

\(= m_{\text{water}}\, s_{\text{water}}(T_{F} - T_{\text{water}})\)

\(= 0.32\ \text{kg} \times 4186\ \text{J} \times (7.8 - 35)\ ^\circ\text{C}\)

\(= -36434.944\) J (here negative sign indicates loss of heat energy)

Heat required to melt ice \(= m_{\text{ice}}L_{f} = 0.1 \times L_{f}\)

Heat required to raise temperature of water (from ice) to final temperature

\(= m_{\text{ice}}\, s\,(T - T_{\text{ice}})\)

\(= 0.1\ \text{kg} \times 4186\ \text{J} \times (7.8 - 0)\ ^\circ\text{C}\)

\(= 3265.08\) J

Heat lost = Heat gained

\(36434.944 = 0.1L_{f} + 3265.08\)

\(L_{f} = \dfrac{36434.944 - 3265.08}{0.1} = 3316.9864\)

\(= 3.31698 \times 10^{5}\) J kg\(^{-1}\)
_note: Three printed slips in the book's own solution, none of which changes the answer: it writes 'Head lost = Heat gained' for 'Heat lost'; it states the units of s_water in the Given block as 'kg K^-1' instead of 'J kg^-1 K^-1'; and it prints the intermediate value as 3316.9864 where the division actually gives 331698.64, immediately before writing the correct final 3.31698 x 10^5 J/kg (the printed intermediate is the answer divided by 100). Arithmetic otherwise verified: 0.32 x 4186 x 27.2 = 36434.944 and 0.1 x 4186 x 7.8 = 3265.08.

stem: What is the rate of energy loss in watt per square metre through a glass window 5 mm thick if outside temperature is \(-20\ ^\circ\)C and inside temperature is 25 \(^\circ\)C? (\(k_{\text{glass}} = 1\) W/m K)
solution:
Given

\(k_{\text{glass}} = 1\) W/m K

\(T_{1} = 25\ ^\circ\)C

\(T_{2} = -20\ ^\circ\)C

\(x = 5\) mm \(= 5 \times 10^{-3}\) m

\(\therefore T_{1} - T_{2} = 25 - (-20)\ ^\circ\text{C} = 45\) K

We have \(P_{\text{cond}} = \dfrac{Q}{t} = kA\dfrac{T_{1} - T_{2}}{x}\).

\(\therefore\) The rate of energy loss per square metre is

\(\dfrac{P_{\text{cond}}}{A} = k\dfrac{T_{1} - T_{2}}{x}\)

\(= 1\ \text{W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \times 45\ \text{K} / (5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m})\)

\(= 9 \times 10^{3}\) W/m\(^{2}\)

stem: The temperature difference between two sides of an iron plate, 2 cm thick, is 10 \(^\circ\)C. Heat is transmitted through the plate at the rate of 600 kcal per minute per square metre at steady state. Find the thermal conductivity of iron.
solution:
Given

\(\dfrac{Q}{At} = 600\ \text{kcal/min m}^{2} = \dfrac{600}{60} = 10\ \text{kcal/s m}^{2}\)

\(x = 2\ \text{cm} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\) m

\(T_{1} - T_{2} = 10\ ^\circ\)C

From Eq. (7.34), we have

\(Q = \dfrac{kA(T_{1} - T_{2})t}{x}\)

\(\therefore k = \dfrac{Q}{At}\dfrac{x}{T_{1} - T_{2}}\)

\(= \dfrac{10\ \text{kcal/s m}^{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}}{10\ ^\circ\text{C}}\)

\(= 0.02\) kcal/m s \(^\circ\)C

stem: Calculate the rate of loss of heat through a glass window of area 1000 cm\(^{2}\) and thickness of 4 mm, when temperature inside is 27 \(^\circ\)C and outside is \(-5\ ^\circ\)C. Coefficient of thermal conductivity of glass is 0.022 cal/ s cm \(^\circ\)C.
solution:
Given

\(A = 1000\ \text{cm}^{2} = 1000 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{2}\)

\(k = 0.022\ \text{cal/ s cm}\ ^\circ\text{C} = 0.022 \times 10^{2}\ \text{cal/m}\ ^\circ\text{C}\)

\(x = 4\ \text{mm} = 0.4 \times 10^{-2}\) m

\(T_{1} = 27\ ^\circ\)C, \(T_{2} = -5\ ^\circ\)C

From Eq. (7.34), we have

\(Q = \dfrac{kA(T_{1} - T_{2})t}{x}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{Q}{t} = \dfrac{kA(T_{1} - T_{2})}{x}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.022 \times 10^{2} \times 1000 \times 10^{-4} \times (27 - (-5))}{0.4 \times 10^{-2}}\)

\(= 1.76 \times 10^{3}\ \text{cal/s} = 1.76\ \text{kcal/s}\)

stem: A metal sphere cools at the rate of 1.6 \(^\circ\)C/min when its temperature is 70 \(^\circ\)C. At what rate will it cool when its temperature is 40 \(^\circ\)C. The temperature of surroundings is 30 \(^\circ\)C.
solution:
Given

\(T_{1} = 70\ ^\circ\)C

\(T_{2} = 40\ ^\circ\)C

\(T_{0} = 30\ ^\circ\)C

\(\left(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\right)_{1} = 1.6\ ^\circ\)C/min

According to Newton's law of cooling, if C is the constant of proportionality

\(\left(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\right)_{1} = C(T_{1} - T_{0})\)

or, \(1.6 = C(70 - 30)\)

\(\therefore C = \dfrac{1.6}{40} = 0.04\) /min

Also \(\left(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\right)_{2} = C(T_{2} - T_{0})\)

\(= 0.04(40 - 30) = 0.4\ ^\circ\)C/min

Thus the rate of cooling drops by a factor of four when the difference in temperature of the metal sphere and its surroundings drops by a factor of four.
